spatial_claims.claim: AB is a straight line bisected at point C, so C is the midpoint of AB
CF is a parallelogrammic figure described on CB (the half of AB)
AD is the complement parallelogram applied to AC within the whole parallelogram on AB, with CF about the diameter
E is a point on AB different from C; AG is applied to segment AE with defect EG similar and similarly situated to CF
EG and CF are about the same diameter DB, by 6.26 (they are similar, similarly situated, and share a common angle at B)
CF (on CB) and EG (on EB) are both parallelograms about the diameter DB in the whole parallelogram on AB
AD is the complement corresponding to CF; AG is the complement corresponding to EG, each complement equaling its opposite complement by 1.43
Since C is the midpoint and E differs from C, EB is not equal to CB
If E lies between A and C, then EB > CB, so EG (on EB) properly contains CF (on CB)
The complement AG plus the gnomon (EG minus CF) equals the complement AD
If E lies between C and B, then EB < CB, so CF (on CB) properly contains EG (on EB)
The complement AD consists of the complement AG plus the gnomon (CF minus EG)
In both cases AD equals AG plus a positive gnomon region, so AD > AG

configuration_map: Line AB with midpoint C. Diameter DB is the diagonal of the whole parallelogram on AB. CF is a parallelogrammic figure about DB sitting on segment CB. E is a variable point on AB (not equal to C). EG is a parallelogrammic figure about the same diameter DB sitting on segment EB, similar and similarly situated to CF. AD is the complement of CF in the whole parallelogram; AG is the complement of EG. When E is between A and C, EB > CB so EG contains CF. When E is between C and B, EB < CB so CF contains EG. In both cases the difference in the about-diameter parallelograms (the gnomon) accounts for the difference in complements, giving AD = AG + gnomon > AG.
pass_reason: The proof makes spatial claims exclusively about point positions on line AB, containment of similar parallelograms about a common diameter, and area decomposition via gnomons. All claims are mutually consistent: the two cases (E between A and C, or E between C and B) correctly determine containment direction, and the gnomon argument properly accounts for the area difference between complements AD and AG. No angle decompositions, no inside/outside triangle claims, and no conflicting point positions are present.
